design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analysis of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT: gum, patch, tablet or lozenge, inhalator, nasal spray, oral spray, combinations, or a choice of products) against placebo or no NRT, in people who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit. Primary outcome: abstinence from smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition available per trial, biochemically confirmed where available; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). 136 studies included; 133 comparisons (131 trials) with 64,640 participants in the main pool. Search July 2017. Adverse events were collected from included and some excluded trials but pooled only for chest pain or palpitations. This version is the NRT-versus-control half of a review that was split in 2017 (the comparisons between forms and doses went to a companion review, Theodoulou et al. 2023).
can_establish: The average relative effect of offering NRT, against placebo or no NRT with the same behavioural support, on abstinence 6 months or more after the start of a quit attempt in people motivated to quit who agreed to take part in randomised trials, overall and by product, support level and setting, as of a July 2017 search.
cannot_establish: Effects in people who are not trying to quit, in people who smoke fewer than about 10 to 15 cigarettes a day (the authors say there is little evidence), in adolescents (two small trials) or in everyday use outside trials; head-to-head differences between products (the product comparisons are indirect subgroups of trials against control); how often side effects occur (adverse events were not pooled except chest pain or palpitations) or whether rare serious harms are raised; whether the pooled size is smaller than estimated because of unpublished trials or manufacturer funding (the authors say it may be); effects beyond the 6 to 24 months of follow-up.

sample.recruitment: Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialised Register (CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and hand-searched conference abstracts), searched 6 July 2017; 1,059 records screened in the latest search. Trials were run in North America (62), Europe (56), Australasia (2), Japan (2), South America (2), Iran (2), several regions (2) and one each in India, Syria, Taiwan and Thailand (Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph). Participants were typically adults who smoked at least 15 cigarettes a day, average age 40 to 50, with similar numbers of men and women, recruited mostly as community volunteers answering advertisements and treated in clinical settings, and from primary care (21 trials), hospitals (13), smoking clinics and settings meant to resemble over-the-counter sale (4 trials). Median trial size 257 (under 50 to over 8,000).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomised or quasi-randomised trials of NRT against placebo or no NRT in people who smoked and were motivated to quit, with a cessation outcome at 6 months or longer (shorter follow-up allowed only for pregnancy trials, and then not in the main analysis). Excluded: trials without a cessation outcome, with follow-up under 6 months, of smoking reduction rather than quitting, trials in which every arm received NRT or NRT was compared with bupropion (moved to other reviews; 34 earlier trials removed), and trials whose control group had access to free NRT.
sample.demographics: Mostly adults; two trials in adolescents (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014); six trials only in pregnant women and four only in women; two trials in African-American participants; single trials in people with alcohol dependence, in methadone-maintained smokers, in people with a history of drug use, in cardiac disease, in hospital patients with cardiac or pulmonary illness and in people with serious mental illness. Average cigarettes a day above 20 in most trials.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. People lost to follow-up or dropping out were counted as still smoking, which the authors say gives conservative absolute quit rates; attrition in NRT groups was generally similar to or lower than in control groups (Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st paragraph). Per-trial attrition sits in the risk-of-bias tables of the Characteristics of included studies, which were searched but not read trial by trial.
sample.selection_effects: A single register was searched, and manufacturers were last written to when the review was first prepared. Trials needed at least 6 months of follow-up and a cessation outcome. Participants were people motivated to quit who accepted randomisation to a possible placebo, typically heavier smokers, and most were treated in clinical or clinic-like settings; in about 60% of trials a drug company funded or supplied the study product (editors' count from the study notes, see key findings). Six trials rest on abstracts, conference presentations or registry entries only. The authors report some funnel-plot asymmetry and say unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing.

exposure.measurement: Allocation to an NRT product or product combination in the trial; adherence was not synthesised (compliance is described trial by trial in the Characteristics tables, which were not read in full).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not recommendations. Gum trials mostly used the 2 mg strength (a few the 4 mg strength for more dependent participants), usually for 2 to 3 months (range 3 weeks to 12 months). Patch trials usually used up to 15 mg over 16 hours or 21 mg over 24 hours for at least 3 weeks to 3 months, with one trial offering a 52.5 mg patch among options. Lozenges, sublingual tablets, nasal and oral sprays and inhalators were each tested in 1 to 8 trials. Seven trials tested a patch plus a short-acting form and seven offered a choice of products.
exposure.polysubstance: Single trials enrolled people with alcohol dependence (Hughes 2003), methadone-maintained smokers (Stein 2013) and people with a history of drug use (Heydari 2013); other substance use was not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence was measured at 6 months or more after the start of treatment (a 6-week window around the 6- or 12-month visit was allowed); 117 trials (87%) biochemically validated self-reported abstinence at longest follow-up, mostly by expired-air carbon monoxide with cut-offs from under 4 to 11 parts per million.

comparison.controls: Placebo product in most trials; 43 trials had no matched placebo (24 gum, 9 patch, 6 choice-of-product, 3 combination and 1 lozenge trial) and two more had both a placebo and a no-placebo control, which were combined.
comparison.matching: Randomisation (adequate allocation concealment reported in 39 trials, 29%); all trials gave both arms the same behavioural support, though the amount of support differed between trials.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomised, so baseline differences are by chance within each trial. Results by baseline dependence, motivation, prior quit attempts, sex or other participant traits were not pooled (subgroup results are uncommon in trial reports); the authors cite two earlier meta-analyses of sex differences that covered a subset of trials.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Whether control participants used NRT or other cessation aids outside the trial was not systematically extracted; one trial was excluded because its control group had access to and used free NRT at high levels.

outcomes.instruments: Abstinence at 6 months or longer (12-month data used where available): sustained abstinence in 89 trials (66%), point prevalence only in 39 (29%), unclear in 6; biochemical validation in 117 trials.
outcomes.validity_norms: Carbon monoxide cut-offs varied from under 4 to 11 ppm; four trials counted people smoking 2 or 3 cigarettes a week as abstinent (dropping them changed nothing); 21 trials did not validate all self-reports (dropping the 17 that never attempted validation changed nothing).
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = the strictest abstinence definition each trial reported, with anyone lost to follow-up counted as smoking. Adverse events were tabulated by study (Appendix 3) and were not pooled except for chest pain or palpitations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Subgroup analyses by product, abstinence definition, support intensity and setting are described as checks on consistency rather than as hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The review authors did not blind themselves to trial results or arms (stated). Within trials, 44 (33%) were judged low risk and 23 (17%) high risk of performance and detection bias, mostly because there was no blinding; the authors did not assess whether blinding held.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI, abstinence at 6 months or longer. All forms pooled: RR 1.55 (1.49 to 1.61), 133 comparisons, 64,640 participants, I2 39%. Gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60), 56, 22,581, I2 40%. Patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75), 51, 25,754, I2 24%. Tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74), 8, 4,439, I2 71%. Inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67), 4, 976, I2 0%. Nasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73), 4, 887, I2 0%. Oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94), 1 trial, 479. Choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52), 7, 8,288, I2 42%. Combinations: patch plus inhalator 1.07 (0.57 to 1.99), 1 trial; patch plus lozenge 1.83 (1.01 to 3.31), 1 trial; patch plus gum 1.15 (0.64 to 2.06), 2 trials; patch plus gum plus lozenge 15.00 (2.00 to 112.54), 1 trial. By setting: community volunteers treated in a medical setting 1.62 (1.53 to 1.72), smoking clinics 1.70 (1.48 to 1.96), primary care 1.50 (1.33 to 1.69), hospitals 1.39 (1.24 to 1.55), over-the-counter-like settings 1.40 (1.26 to 1.55), antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62). Sensitivity (analyses not shown in the review): excluding high-risk trials 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); validated abstinence only 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70). Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 trials, 11,074 participants. Absolute figures (Summary of findings table): 105 per 1,000 without NRT against 162 (156 to 168) with NRT; 40 against 62 (60 to 64) with limited support; 150 against 232 (224 to 242) with intensive support. No tau-squared or prediction interval (fixed-effect model).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroup analyses by abstinence definition (gum, patch), intensity of behavioural support (gum, patch) and setting, plus a meta-regression of setting by product type; no meta-regression on participant characteristics.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol first published in Issue 2, 1996. The History table records later changes of scope or method: effect measure changed from odds ratio to risk ratio (2007), adverse-events table added (2012), and in 2017 the review was split, moving comparisons between NRT types and with bupropion elsewhere. This version has no section comparing the review with its protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods name no selective-reporting domain among the risk-of-bias items (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, other), so selective outcome reporting was not assessed per trial. Adverse events were recorded where reported and not synthesised because reporting varied. The sensitivity analyses are reported in a sentence each, without a table. The review does not say whether registered primary outcomes were compared with published ones.
analysis.power: The main pool is large (64,640 participants). Individual trials were often small: in 73% of trials the interval for the RR included 1, and 12 trials had lower quit rates with NRT (all intervals crossed 1). Product subgroups with the highest estimates rest on few trials: inhalator 4 trials (976 participants), nasal spray 4 (887), oral spray 1 (479), and the 15.00 estimate is one trial in which one control participant quit.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across randomised trials of people motivated to quit, offering any form of NRT was followed by more people abstinent at 6 months or longer than placebo or no NRT: 162 against 105 per 1,000 overall (about 6 more in 100), about 2 more in 100 with limited behavioural support and about 8 more in 100 with intensive support (editors' arithmetic from the Summary of findings table). The relative effect (RR about 1.5 to 1.6) was similar across gum, patch and lozenge or tablet, with wider and higher estimates for inhalator, nasal and oral spray from few trials, and similar across support levels and most settings, though not significant in four antenatal-clinic trials (RR 1.22, 0.92 to 1.62). Restricting to low-risk or placebo-controlled trials gave similar estimates. Side effects were mainly local irritation at the site of use; chest pain or palpitations were reported by 2.5% with NRT against 1.4% with control (OR 1.88). Serious adverse events were not pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and authors' conclusions state high-quality evidence that all licensed forms help, that NRT raises quitting by 50% to 60% regardless of setting, that further research is very unlikely to change the estimate, that the form of delivery is unrelated to effectiveness, and that serious adverse events were extremely rare. The plain language summary adds that there is no evidence NRT raises the risk of heart attacks. Gaps: (1) regardless of setting sits beside a non-significant estimate in antenatal clinics; (2) unrelated to effectiveness rests on indirect subgroup comparisons whose estimates run from 1.49 (gum) to 2.48 (oral spray, one trial), so it is a statement of no demonstrated difference, not of equivalence, and the companion review (Theodoulou 2023) is the direct evidence; (3) relative gains of 50% to 60% are given without absolute numbers in the abstract (the Summary of findings gives them); (4) high quality is the authors' GRADE judgement even though only 12 of 136 trials were low risk of bias, the funnel plot is asymmetric, about 60% of trials involved a manufacturer and the authors themselves say the true effect may be smaller; (5) the safety statements go beyond the data: adverse events were deliberately not pooled, serious events were not counted across trials, the review has no heart-attack outcome, and the text calls events at 2.5% and 1.4% extremely rare; (6) the abstract's wording about quitting applies to people motivated to quit in trials, while observational studies of everyday use that the review discusses give mixed results (the authors attribute this to confounding by choice of treatment).

timeline.event: First version of this Cochrane review (Silagy et al.); the number of included trials has more than doubled since, and the authors state the pooled estimate has stayed stable.
Update changes the effect measure from odds ratio to risk ratio and modifies some comparisons.
Update adds a table of adverse events by study.
Review split: this version covers NRT against control; comparisons between forms, doses and schedules move to a companion review.
This version (Hartmann-Boyce et al.), search July 2017; marked stable, with no further updates planned.
Companion Cochrane review of different forms, doses and durations of NRT (Theodoulou et al.), read for the same claims.
Cochrane living review of electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation, which uses NRT as a comparator; read separately.

replication.where_it_stands: The main finding that NRT, offered with the same support as control, raises abstinence at 6 months or more is consistent across 20 years of trials and is not an artefact of any single trial; the size, however, comes from trials in people motivated to quit, often with clinic support, and about 60% involved a manufacturer. A 2023 companion review (Theodoulou et al.) compares forms head to head and finds combinations better than single forms and fast-acting forms similar to patches. Observational work on everyday use is mixed and confounded by who chooses NRT. Primary trials inside this pool (for example Anthenelli 2016, Jorenby 1999, Shiffman 2009) must not be counted as independent support beside this review.

funding.funder: National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) infrastructure funding for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group; NIHR School for Primary Care Research (support for the Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford, the group's editorial base); one author (JHB) funded in part by the NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre. No industry funding of the review is declared.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (CB) was involved in a trial of pre-cessation NRT (Bullen 2010), which this review lists among trials contributing adverse-event data only; the other authors declare none known. Funding of the included trials, from their notes in the Characteristics of included studies (editors' count; the review did not analyse by funder): of the 136 included entries, about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product (for example Pharmacia, Kabi, Elan, Marion Merrell Dow, Ciba-Geigy, Glaxo, Novartis, Pfizer, McNeil, Lundbeck, Leo; some of these supplied product only, such as Ahluwalia 2006, Oncken 2007 and Piper 2009), about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, and about 15 report no funding source. The authors cite a meta-analysis (Etter 2007) in which gum and patch trials with pharmaceutical funding had slightly higher effect sizes, and say the magnitude of NRT's effect may be smaller than their estimates suggest.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not part of the page text read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: A comparison of effect sizes between trials funded by manufacturers and trials funded independently (a funder-stratified meta-analysis, which this review did not run); registered trials with all outcomes and adverse events reported by arm; pragmatic trials of NRT given without clinic support, in people not planning to quit and in people smoking fewer than 10 cigarettes a day, with follow-up beyond 12 months and with serious adverse events counted in a prespecified way.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People who smoked and were motivated to quit; licensed NRT forms; placebo or no-NRT control; abstinence at 6 months or more plus adverse events; randomised and quasi-randomised trials.
A Cochrane protocol was published in 1996 and the History table lists later changes, including the 2017 split, but this version does not compare the review with its protocol or justify each change.
Randomised and quasi-randomised trials, with a sensitivity analysis for quasi-randomisation; restriction to trials is the standard design for an efficacy question, with no separate justification.

Register built from CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and hand-searched conference abstracts, strategy in Appendix 1, no date or language limits, searched July 2017 (within a year of publication). Not stated: searching reference lists of included trials; manufacturers were last contacted when the review was first prepared; trial registries are mentioned only in the Discussion.
Two authors screened independently in the last two updates; earlier updates used one screener, so older selections were not duplicated.
Two authors extracted independently, disagreements settled by discussion or a third person; translators used for non-English reports.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Characteristics of excluded studies lists each study with its reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Each trial has a table of country, recruitment, participants, interventions, outcomes, validation, funding notes and risk-of-bias judgements.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data and other bias, in a table per trial; the Methods name no selective-reporting domain, so selection of the reported result was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: The Notes field of each trial gives funders and suppliers or says not reported (about 15 trials).

Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios with I2 reported (39% overall; 71% in the lozenge subgroup, traced to one trial); placebo-controlled and no-placebo trials pooled but checked in a placebo-only sensitivity analysis; loss to follow-up counted as smoking. Judged met on balance, a close call: no random-effects check despite moderate heterogeneity.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk trials, keeping only the 12 low-risk trials, excluding unvalidated trials and keeping placebo-controlled trials only, all consistent (reported without tables).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The GRADE footnote and the Limitations section state that most trials were unclear or high risk and that the estimate was unchanged in the sensitivity analyses.
I2 reported by subgroup; the high value in the lozenge subgroup attributed to one trial; subgroups by abstinence definition, support and setting.
A funnel plot (Figure 4, an image) was inspected and its asymmetry discussed with the pharmaceutical-funding finding of Etter 2007; no statistical test.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations of interest are given; no industry funding of the review.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no. Three critical items are only partly met (2, 4 and 9), which AMSTAR 2 does not count as flaws, so the mechanical rating is high confidence. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good the trials are: most of the 136 trials were unclear (88) or high (36) risk of bias, six rest on abstracts or registry entries, selective reporting was not assessed, the funnel plot is asymmetric and about 60% of trials involved a manufacturer. The authors' own sensitivity analyses (low-risk trials only, validated abstinence only, placebo-controlled only) give RR 1.53 to 1.62 against 1.55, which is why the efficacy estimate is usable. May be cited for: the pooled efficacy of NRT against control and its absolute size under limited and intensive support; product-level estimates as indirect subgroup results; the descriptive list of local side effects; the funnel-plot and industry caveats. May not be cited for: which form works best (use the companion review), everyday-use effectiveness, how often side effects occur, or whether NRT is safe.

key_findings.finding: Any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer: pooled RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49 to 1.61), 133 comparisons from 131 trials, 64,640 participants, fixed-effect, I2 39%. The authors rate the evidence high certainty (GRADE).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1
key_findings.note: The Results say 131 trials (133 comparisons); the abstract and Table 1 say 133 studies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Absolute figures in the Summary of findings table: without NRT 105 per 1,000 abstinent, with NRT 162 per 1,000 (156 to 168); with limited behavioural support 40 against 62 per 1,000 (60 to 64); with intensive support 150 against 232 per 1,000 (224 to 242). Editors' arithmetic: about 6, 2 and 8 more people in 100 abstinent.

RR by product (comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60; 56; 22,581; I2 40%); patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75; 51; 25,754; I2 24%); tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74; 8; 4,439; I2 71%); inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67; 4; 976); intranasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73; 4; 887); oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94; 1 trial; 479); choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52; 7; 8,288); patch plus inhalator 1.07 (0.57 to 1.99; 1); patch plus lozenge 1.83 (1.01 to 3.31; 1); patch plus gum 1.15 (0.64 to 2.06; 2); patch plus gum plus lozenge 15.00 (2.00 to 112.54; 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, table after the 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
key_findings.note: The 15.00 estimate is one trial in which one control participant quit. Subgroup estimates are indirect comparisons of trials against control, not head-to-head.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity and single trials: the lozenge or tablet subgroup had I2 71%, driven by one new trial with RR 1.08 (Fraser 2014). Twelve trials had lower quit rates with NRT than control (all intervals crossed 1) and in a further 73% of trials the interval included 1. One large patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease (Joseph 1996) found quit rates of 14% with active patch and 11% with placebo at 6 months, and 10% and 12% at 48 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Quit rates in control groups rose with behavioural support: gum trials 3.5% (low-intensity support), 9% (high-intensity individual) and 11.7% (group-based); patch trials 9.0%, 9.5% and 17.0%. Relative effects were reported as similar across support levels. By setting, control quit rates were 8.4% (over-the-counter-like), 6.9% (primary care), 14.3% (smoking clinics), 9.3% (antenatal), 12.5% (community volunteers in a medical setting) and 12.3% (hospitals).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to intensity of behavioural support; Sensitivity to treatment settings, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Data and analyses give gum RR 1.66 (1.46 to 1.88) with low-intensity support, 1.32 (1.18 to 1.49) with high-intensity individual support and 1.57 (1.40 to 1.76) with group support; the text says no significant difference between groups.

key_findings.finding: RR by setting: community volunteers treated in a medical setting 1.62 (1.53 to 1.72; 65 trials; 24,597); smoking clinics 1.70 (1.48 to 1.96; 12; 3,300); primary care 1.50 (1.33 to 1.69; 24; 11,974); hospitals 1.39 (1.24 to 1.55; 13; 7,037); over-the-counter-like settings 1.40 (1.26 to 1.55; 9; 13,163); antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62; 4; 1,675), the only setting without a statistically significant effect.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 4

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses (not shown in the review): excluding high-risk trials RR 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); excluding trials without biochemical validation 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled trials only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to risk of bias and study methods

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: 12 trials low risk in all domains, 36 high risk in at least one domain, the rest unclear. Allocation procedures adequately reported in 39 trials (29%); 44 trials (33%) low and 23 (17%) high risk of performance or detection bias; 43 trials had no matched placebo; six trials rest on abstracts, conference presentations or registry entries; 117 trials (87%) validated abstinence biochemically; follow-up was only 6 months in 15 gum, 19 patch, 4 combination and 1 lozenge trial.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Adverse events were not pooled, because the nature, timing and duration of symptoms were reported too variably; main events are tabulated by trial in Appendix 3. Local effects reported: gum, hiccoughs, gastrointestinal disturbance, jaw pain and orodental problems; patch, skin sensitivity and irritation (up to 54% in one cited source), usually mild; inhalator and nasal or oral spray, irritation at the site of use (throat irritation, coughing, oral burning; nasal irritation and runny nose; hiccoughs); sublingual tablets, hiccoughs, burning in the mouth, sore throat, cough, dry lips and mouth ulcers. Adolescents reported similar events to adults.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Appendix 3

key_findings.finding: Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 included and excluded trials, 11,074 participants, with 2.5% of NRT groups and 1.4% of control groups affected. An earlier meta-analysis (Mills 2010) found OR 2.06 (1.51 to 2.82) in 12 studies. The authors describe the events as extremely rare and report no evidence of an excess of serious cardiac problems.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 6
key_findings.note: The text calls events at 2.5% and 1.4% extremely rare.

key_findings.finding: Cardiac disease and pregnancy: in one patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease serious adverse events were not more common with the patch, and cardiovascular events such as worse angina (about 16% of participants) did not differ by arm (Joseph 1996). A cited network meta-analysis (Mills 2014) found more cardiovascular events with NRT overall (RR 2.29, 1.39 to 3.82), driven by lower-level events such as tachycardia, and no significant excess of serious cardiac events (printed RR 1.95, 0.26 to 4.30). Six trials in pregnant women did not detect significant increases in serious adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Figures from Mills 2014 are quoted from another review and were not checked.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy (six trials): abstinence at end of pregnancy RR 1.32 (1.04 to 1.69; 2,129 participants); at longest postpartum follow-up RR 1.29 (0.90 to 1.86; four trials, 1,675 participants). The review refers readers to a separate Cochrane review for pregnancy.
key_findings.locator: Data and analyses, Comparison 5; Discussion › Trials in special populations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adolescents: two small trials (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014) did not detect an effect on quitting at 6 months or longer, and a separate Cochrane review of young people also found none, with wide intervals. The authors state there is little evidence about NRT in people smoking fewer than 10 to 15 cigarettes a day.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Trials in special populations, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing; a funnel plot shows some asymmetry; a cited meta-analysis (Etter 2007) found nicotine gum and patch trials with pharmaceutical funding had slightly higher effect sizes on average; the authors conclude that the magnitude of effectiveness may be smaller than their estimates. They did not repeat their letter to manufacturers after the first version.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence base, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1 footnote 2
key_findings.note: Summary of findings footnotes give the authors' reason for not downgrading the high rating: most studies were at unclear or high risk of bias but restricting to low-risk trials did not alter the effect, and given the large number of trials the asymmetry does not suggest that adding smaller trials with lower risk ratios would change the results significantly.

key_findings.finding: Funding of the included trials (editors' count from the Notes field of the Characteristics of included studies, by company-name matching and reading; the review itself did not analyse by funder): of 136 included entries, about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product, about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, and about 15 report no source.
key_findings.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count)
key_findings.note: Approximate. Some entries are two halves of one trial (Shiffman 2002; Shiffman 2009), and some company links are product supply only.

key_findings.finding: Everyday use outside trials: the review discusses observational studies finding no difference or lower quit rates among people who used over-the-counter NRT (California surveys, 2002; a UK prospective cohort, OR 0.69, 0.49 to 0.94, against no pharmacotherapy or service) and others finding higher quit rates among people who used NRT (two multi-country cohorts, in one only for patches); it attributes these differences to residual confounding, because people chose their own treatment.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Intensity of additional support and treatment setting, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Follow-up: trials needed at least 6 months, most reported at least 12 months from the start of treatment, and the relative effect was not smaller in trials with longer follow-up. The authors cite work suggesting the relative effect falls once treatment stops but does not change beyond a year (12 trials), with later relapse shrinking the absolute difference.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Limitations of the evidence base, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Methods in brief: Specialised Register searched 6 July 2017 (CENTRAL issue 11 2016, MEDLINE to May 2017, Embase to week 24 2017, PsycINFO to May 2017; no language restriction); duplicate screening and extraction; Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios; GRADE for the main outcome only.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search methods for identification of studies; Data collection and analysis

reporting_issues.issue: The number of trials in the main pool is given three ways. The abstract and Table 1 say 133 studies; the Results say Analysis 1.1 included 131 trials (133 comparisons); and the trial counts by product in Description of studies (56 gum, 51 patch, 8 tablet or lozenge, 7 choice, 4 spray, 4 inhalator, 2 patch and gum, 1 oral spray, 1 patch and inhalator, 1 patch and lozenge, 1 patch, gum and lozenge) add up to 136, the number of included studies. The text explains that some trials contribute to more than one subgroup and that two studies were split into four comparisons.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote 133 comparisons (131 trials) rather than 133 trials; the product-level counts cannot be added.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's worked absolute effects do not reconcile with the risk ratio or with each other: an increase of 2% to 3% on a 3% to 5% baseline is given an NNTB of 56 (2 to 3 per 100 would give about 33 to 50), and a further 8% on a 15% baseline is given an NNTB of 11 (editors' arithmetic: 100 divided by 8 is about 12.5; a baseline of 15% with RR 1.55 gives about 8 more per 100).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Summary of findings table (105 against 162 per 1,000; 40 against 62; 150 against 232) for absolute numbers, not the Discussion's NNTBs.

reporting_issues.issue: Events at 2.5% (NRT) and 1.4% (control) are called extremely rare, and the abstract calls serious adverse events extremely rare although serious events were not counted across trials.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Abstract
reporting_issues.consequence: The reassuring wording is stronger than the data; the claim states the percentages instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions say NRT raises quitting regardless of setting, yet the antenatal-clinic subgroup (four trials, 1,675 participants) has RR 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62), which the text itself notes is the one setting without a significant effect; and they state the form of delivery is unrelated to effectiveness while product subgroup estimates run from 1.49 to 2.48 with wide intervals and few trials for the higher ones.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice; Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat regardless of setting and unrelated to the form as no demonstrated difference in these indirect comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The Mills 2014 serious cardiac events estimate is printed as RR 1.95 (95% CI 0.26 to 4.30). A ratio estimate that sits well above the centre of its interval on the log scale (about 1.06) may reflect a typing error in the upper limit or a skewed credible interval from a network meta-analysis; it could not be checked here.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is not used in any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages are calculated on different denominators: 117 trials is given as 87% (which fits 134 trials), 44 trials as 33% (fits 133) and 89 trials as 66% (fits about 134).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 3rd to 6th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote counts rather than percentages.
